description: What does the bias-variance trade-off describe?
explanation: Simple models err by being systematically wrong (bias); flexible ones err by being over-sensitive to the training sample (variance). Reducing one tends to raise the other.
choice0: The tension between being systematically wrong and being over-sensitive to the sample
choice1: The trade-off between training time and accuracy
choice2: The trade-off between the number of rows and columns
choice3: The difference between training and test set sizes

description: A model gives very different results each time it is trained on a different sample. What does that indicate?
explanation: Sensitivity to the particular training sample is high variance, the signature of an overly flexible model.
choice0: High bias
choice1: High variance
choice2: Data leakage
choice3: Class imbalance

description: How does increasing model complexity usually affect bias and variance?
explanation: More flexibility lets the model fit the true shape better, lowering bias, but makes it track the sample more closely, raising variance.
choice0: Both rise
choice1: Both fall
choice2: Bias falls and variance rises
choice3: Bias rises and variance falls

description: How does gathering more training data typically affect variance?
explanation: More data makes the training sample more representative, so the fitted model varies less from sample to sample.
choice0: It reduces variance
choice1: It increases variance
choice2: It has no effect on variance
choice3: It removes bias entirely

description: Why can accuracy be actively misleading on a dataset that is 98 percent negative?
explanation: A model predicting negative every time scores 98 percent while identifying none of the cases of interest.
choice0: Because accuracy cannot be computed on imbalanced data
choice1: Because always predicting the majority class scores 98 percent while finding nothing
choice2: Because accuracy only applies to regression
choice3: Because the test set will contain no positives

description: When is precision-recall generally more informative than a ROC curve?
explanation: With a heavily imbalanced positive class, the large number of true negatives flatters the false positive rate, so ROC looks better than the model is.
choice0: When the positive class is rare, since ROC is flattered by many true negatives
choice1: When the classes are perfectly balanced
choice2: When the model is a regressor
choice3: When the test set is very large

description: What does an AUC of 0.5 tell you about a classifier?
explanation: It ranks positives above negatives no better than chance.
choice0: It is perfectly accurate
choice1: It is perfectly wrong
choice2: It performs no better than random guessing
choice3: It has not finished training

description: What is model calibration?
explanation: A calibrated model outputs probabilities that match reality: among cases it rates at 0.7, about 70 percent should be positive.
choice0: Its predicted probabilities match the real frequencies
choice1: Its accuracy matches its recall
choice2: Its training and test scores are equal
choice3: Its features are all on the same scale

description: Why can a highly accurate model still be poorly calibrated?
explanation: Ranking cases correctly is a different property from stating the right probability, so a model can order well but be systematically over-confident.
choice0: Because accuracy is measured on the training set
choice1: Because calibration only applies to regression
choice2: Because accuracy always exceeds calibration
choice3: Because ordering cases correctly is separate from stating the right probability

description: Why is a random split wrong for time series data?
explanation: Random splitting lets the model train on the future and predict the past, which cannot happen in practice and inflates the score.
choice0: It lets the model train on future data and predict the past
choice1: Time series data cannot be split at all
choice2: It always produces uneven split sizes
choice3: It removes the seasonal pattern

description: How should time series data be split instead?
explanation: Split by time, training on earlier periods and validating on later ones, mirroring how the model will be used.
choice0: Alternate rows between train and test
choice1: Train on earlier periods and validate on later ones
choice2: Sort by the target and split in half
choice3: Use every third row for testing

description: A dataset has several rows per patient. Why is a plain random split a problem?
explanation: Rows from the same patient can land in both parts, so the model recognises the patient rather than learning the condition.
choice0: It makes the split sizes unequal
choice1: It removes patients with few rows
choice2: Rows from one patient land on both sides, so the model recognises the patient
choice3: Patient identifiers cannot be used as features

description: What does grouped cross-validation ensure?
explanation: All rows sharing a group, such as one patient or one customer, stay entirely within one fold.
choice0: All rows of a group stay within a single fold
choice1: Each fold has the same number of rows
choice2: Each fold contains every class equally
choice3: Groups are removed before validation

description: What is the risk of tuning many hyperparameters against the same validation set?
explanation: Repeated selection fits the model to that particular split, so the validation score becomes optimistic and stops predicting real performance.
choice0: Training becomes prohibitively slow
choice1: The score becomes optimistic because the choices are fitted to that split
choice2: The model can no longer be retrained
choice3: The validation set shrinks each time

description: What is nested cross-validation for?
explanation: An inner loop tunes the settings and an outer loop measures performance, so the reported score is not contaminated by the tuning.
choice0: Separating the tuning loop from the loop that estimates performance
choice1: Running two models at once
choice2: Splitting each feature into folds
choice3: Validating two datasets simultaneously

description: How does random search often compare with an exhaustive grid search?
explanation: When only a few hyperparameters matter, random search explores those dimensions more finely for the same budget.
choice0: It is always less effective
choice1: It only works for neural networks
choice2: It often finds comparable settings faster when only a few parameters matter
choice3: It guarantees the global optimum

description: What does resampling an imbalanced training set do, and what must you avoid?
explanation: Resampling rebalances the training data, but the validation and test sets must keep the real proportions or the estimate becomes meaningless.
choice0: It rebalances training data; the test set must keep the real proportions
choice1: It rebalances the test set; training must stay imbalanced
choice2: It removes the need for a validation set
choice3: It converts the problem into regression

description: What does class weighting do?
explanation: It makes errors on the rare class cost more during training, so the model stops ignoring it.
choice0: It removes examples of the common class
choice1: It makes mistakes on the rare class cost more during training
choice2: It duplicates rare examples in the test set
choice3: It changes the evaluation metric automatically

description: What does feature importance tell you, and what does it not?
explanation: It shows which features the model relies on, which is not the same as showing what causes the outcome.
choice0: It proves which features cause the outcome
choice1: It shows which features have the most missing values
choice2: It shows what the model relies on, which is not evidence of causation
choice3: It ranks features by their variance

description: Why is correlation between two features a problem for interpreting their importance?
explanation: When features carry the same information the model can use either, so importance gets split arbitrarily between them.
choice0: The model can use either one, so importance is split arbitrarily
choice1: Correlated features cannot be used at all
choice2: It always causes the model to overfit
choice3: It makes the loss function undefined

description: What does a partial dependence plot show?
explanation: It shows how the predicted outcome changes as one feature varies, averaging over the others.
choice0: How the loss changed during training
choice1: How the prediction changes as one feature varies, averaging over the rest
choice2: The distribution of a feature in the training set
choice3: Which examples the model got wrong

description: Why is an accurate model still not evidence that a feature causes the outcome?
explanation: A model exploits any reliable association, including ones driven by a common cause or by the way the data was collected.
choice0: Because models never use causal features
choice1: Because accuracy is measured on the test set
choice2: Because causation requires a larger sample
choice3: Because it exploits any reliable association, whatever produced it

description: Why must preprocessing steps be fitted inside the cross-validation loop?
explanation: Fitting a scaler or imputer on all the data lets information from the held-out fold influence training, inflating the score.
choice0: Otherwise information from the held-out fold leaks into training
choice1: Otherwise preprocessing runs too slowly
choice2: Because preprocessing cannot handle folds
choice3: Because each fold needs a different algorithm

description: What is the role of a pipeline object in preventing leakage?
explanation: It binds preprocessing and the model into one unit, so every fit happens on training data only and is reapplied consistently.
choice0: It speeds up training by caching results
choice1: It binds preprocessing to the model so each fit sees only training data
choice2: It selects the best algorithm automatically
choice3: It stores the dataset in memory

description: Why is a target-encoded categorical feature especially prone to leakage?
explanation: The encoding is computed from the target itself, so unless it is fitted within each fold the label bleeds directly into the feature.
choice0: Because categories cannot be encoded numerically
choice1: Because it creates too many columns
choice2: Because it is computed from the target, which bleeds the label into the feature
choice3: Because it requires the test set to be sorted

description: What does dimensionality reduction such as PCA try to preserve?
explanation: It compresses many correlated features into fewer combinations that retain most of the variation in the data.
choice0: Most of the variation, using fewer combined features
choice1: The exact original values of every feature
choice2: The class labels of each example
choice3: The order of the rows

description: What is the main interpretability cost of using PCA?
explanation: The new components are blends of the originals, so a coefficient no longer refers to any real-world quantity.
choice0: The model can no longer be evaluated
choice1: The components are blends, so they no longer map to real-world quantities
choice2: The features can no longer be scaled
choice3: The target variable is transformed as well

description: When is it reasonable to drop a feature with a very large share of missing values?
explanation: When the missingness itself carries no signal and too little remains to estimate a reliable effect.
choice0: Always, whenever anything is missing
choice1: Never, since dropping data is always wrong
choice2: When the pattern of missingness carries no signal and too little data remains
choice3: Only if the feature is categorical

description: Why can the fact that a value is missing be informative in itself?
explanation: Missingness often reflects something real, such as a question people skip when the honest answer is awkward, so a flag can be predictive.
choice0: Missingness can reflect something real and be predictive on its own
choice1: Missing values always indicate corrupted data
choice2: Models automatically treat missingness as a category
choice3: It means the row should always be dropped

description: What is the practical difference between batch and stochastic gradient descent?
explanation: Batch uses the whole dataset for each step, giving smooth but expensive updates; stochastic uses one or a few examples, giving noisy but fast ones.
choice0: Batch uses one example per step, stochastic uses all of them
choice1: Batch uses the whole dataset per step, stochastic uses one or a few
choice2: They differ only in the learning rate
choice3: Batch is for classification, stochastic for regression

description: Why is a decreasing learning rate schedule often used?
explanation: Large steps early cover ground quickly, while smaller steps later let the model settle near the minimum instead of bouncing around it.
choice0: Large steps explore quickly, small steps settle near the minimum
choice1: It reduces the size of the training set
choice2: It prevents the loss from being computed
choice3: It guarantees the global optimum is found

description: What does a training loss that keeps falling while validation loss rises indicate?
explanation: The model has begun memorising the training data: the classic overfitting signature, and the point to stop.
choice0: The learning rate is too low
choice1: The validation set is too small
choice2: Overfitting has begun and training should stop
choice3: The model is still underfitting

description: Why is it useful to plot a learning curve against training set size?
explanation: If performance is still improving as data grows, more data will help; if it has flattened, the model or features are the limit.
choice0: It shows whether more data would help or the model itself is the limit
choice1: It shows which features are most important
choice2: It replaces the need for cross-validation
choice3: It measures how fast the model predicts

description: What distinguishes L1 from L2 regularisation in practice?
explanation: L1 can drive coefficients exactly to zero, effectively selecting features, while L2 shrinks them toward zero without eliminating them.
choice0: L2 sets coefficients to zero, L1 only shrinks them
choice1: L1 can zero out coefficients, effectively selecting features; L2 only shrinks them
choice2: They are mathematically identical
choice3: L1 applies to classification and L2 to regression

description: What happens if the regularisation strength is set far too high?
explanation: The penalty dominates the fit, forcing the model toward a trivial one that underfits badly.
choice0: The model is forced toward triviality and underfits
choice1: The model overfits more severely
choice2: Training fails with an error
choice3: The learning rate is ignored

description: What is the core idea behind bagging?
explanation: Train many models on different bootstrap samples and average them, which cuts variance without adding much bias.
choice0: Train models one after another, each fixing the last ones errors
choice1: Combine models of different types by voting on their confidence
choice2: Train many models on different samples and average them to cut variance
choice3: Train one model and reuse it on several datasets

description: What is the core idea behind boosting?
explanation: Models are trained in sequence, each concentrating on the examples the previous ones got wrong.
choice0: Models are trained in sequence, each focusing on the previous errors
choice1: Models are trained independently and averaged
choice2: The largest model is selected and the rest discarded
choice3: The dataset is boosted by duplicating every row

description: Why is boosting typically more prone to overfitting than bagging?
explanation: Because it keeps fitting the residual errors, it will eventually start fitting noise if the number of rounds is not controlled.
choice0: Because it uses fewer models
choice1: Because it keeps fitting residual errors and will eventually fit noise
choice2: Because it cannot use a validation set
choice3: Because it ignores the majority class

description: What is training-serving skew?
explanation: The features computed in production differ subtly from those used in training, so the model sees inputs unlike anything it learned from.
choice0: Features are computed differently in production than in training
choice1: The model file is a different version in production
choice2: Training takes longer than serving
choice3: The test set was too small

description: Why is a shadow deployment useful before switching to a new model?
explanation: The new model scores live traffic without acting on it, so its behaviour can be compared against the current one at no risk.
choice0: It halves the serving cost
choice1: It scores live traffic without acting, allowing a risk-free comparison
choice2: It removes the need for a test set
choice3: It retrains the model on production data automatically

description: What kind of drift is it when the input distribution changes but the underlying relationship does not?
explanation: That is covariate shift: the features move, the mapping from features to target does not.
choice0: Concept drift
choice1: Label drift
choice2: Covariate shift
choice3: Data leakage

description: What kind of drift is it when the relationship between features and target itself changes?
explanation: That is concept drift, and it usually requires retraining because the old mapping is no longer correct.
choice0: Concept drift
choice1: Covariate shift
choice2: Sampling bias
choice3: Overfitting

description: Why does removing a protected attribute like ethnicity not guarantee a fair model?
explanation: Other features act as proxies, so the model can reconstruct the attribute indirectly from postcode, name or purchase history.
choice0: Because the attribute is still stored in the database
choice1: Because other features act as proxies and reconstruct it indirectly
choice2: Because fairness only applies to regression
choice3: Because the model needs it to make predictions

description: Why can a model trained on historical hiring decisions perpetuate past discrimination?
explanation: It learns to reproduce the decisions in its training data, including the biased ones, and presents them as objective.
choice0: It reproduces the biased decisions it was trained on, with a veneer of objectivity
choice1: Because hiring data is always incomplete
choice2: Because classification cannot handle people data
choice3: Because the model has too few features

description: What is a feedback loop in a deployed model?
explanation: The models predictions change behaviour, which changes the data it is later retrained on, entrenching its own assumptions.
choice0: The model reports its accuracy back to the training system
choice1: Users can correct individual predictions
choice2: The model is retrained on a fixed schedule
choice3: Predictions influence behaviour, which shapes the data the model later learns from

description: Why should the evaluation metric be chosen before modelling begins?
explanation: Picking the metric afterwards invites choosing whichever one flatters the result, and the metric should reflect the real-world cost of each error.
choice0: Choosing afterwards invites picking whichever metric flatters the result
choice1: Because metrics cannot be changed once training starts
choice2: Because the algorithm depends on the metric name
choice3: Because the test set is built from the metric

description: What is the value of a held-out set that is used exactly once?
explanation: A set never used for any decision gives an honest final estimate, since nothing about the model was chosen to suit it.
choice0: It trains faster than a reused set
choice1: It gives an honest final estimate, since no choices were fitted to it
choice2: It can be smaller than the training set
choice3: It removes the need for cross-validation

description: When a model performs far worse in production than in testing, what should you suspect first?
explanation: A gap that large usually means the test data was not representative or something leaked, rather than the algorithm being wrong.
choice0: The learning rate was too high
choice1: The model needs more layers
choice2: The test data was unrepresentative, or something leaked during training
choice3: The production hardware is too slow

description: Why is a reproducible pipeline, with fixed random seeds and recorded data versions, worth the effort?
explanation: Without it you cannot tell whether a change in score came from your change or from randomness and shifting data.
choice0: Otherwise you cannot tell whether a score change came from your change or from noise
choice1: Because random seeds improve accuracy
choice2: Because it is required for cross-validation
choice3: Because it reduces the size of the model file

description: How should the decision threshold be chosen when a false negative costs ten times a false positive?
explanation: Pick the threshold that minimises the expected cost given those weights, rather than defaulting to 0.5, which assumes the two errors are equally bad.
hint: The default 0.5 assumes both mistakes cost the same.
choice0: Choose the threshold that minimises expected cost under those weights
choice1: Always leave it at 0.5, which is statistically optimal
choice2: Set it to 0.9 so the model is more confident
choice3: Retrain the model until accuracy exceeds 90 percent
